ia.name: Portfolio of three commentaries

criteria.name: A · Diagrams (3 marks × 3 commentaries)
look: Diagrams that are relevant to the article and fully labelled (axes, curves, equilibria)
Diagrams adapted to the article's context, e.g. shifts shown and real names or prices used
Each diagram fully explained in the text, not just drawn

criteria.name: B · Terminology (2 marks × 3 commentaries)
look: Economic terms relevant to the article used throughout
Terms used precisely and correctly, not just listed or defined

criteria.name: C · Application and analysis (3 marks × 3 commentaries)
look: Economic theory applied directly to the events in the article
Analysis that follows a clear chain of cause and effect
Evidence from the article used to support each step

criteria.name: D · Key concept (3 marks × 3 commentaries)
look: One key concept clearly identified for each commentary, and a different one each time
The concept linked to the article in a developed, explicit way, not only named in the introduction

criteria.name: E · Evaluation (3 marks × 3 commentaries)
look: Judgements supported by reasoning and evidence
Consideration of stakeholders, short versus long run, assumptions and alternatives
A justified conclusion that answers the issue raised by the article

criteria.name: F · Rubric requirements (whole portfolio)
look: Each commentary based on a different unit of the syllabus (not unit 1)
Each article from a different, appropriate published source
Each article published no earlier than one year before the commentary was written

checklist: Three commentaries, each on a different syllabus unit (micro, macro, global economy)
Each commentary is 800 words or fewer (excluding diagrams, labels, headings, footnotes, references)
Each article comes from a different source and is no more than a year old when you write about it
A different key concept is chosen for each commentary and named on the cover sheet
Every commentary has at least one accurate, fully labelled diagram tailored to the article
Each diagram is explained in the text and linked to the article's events
Key terms are used precisely (and defined only where it helps the analysis)
Evaluation weighs stakeholders, short-run versus long-run effects and possible alternatives
A copy of the article (with the relevant parts highlighted) is attached to each commentary
Cover sheet includes title, source, dates, word count, unit and key concept

examTips: Draw a fully labelled diagram whenever you can: titled axes, labelled curves, equilibrium points and arrows showing shifts, then explain it in words.
In Paper 2 and Paper 3, always refer to the text or data: name the country or firm and quote figures from the extract.
Show all working in calculations and give units (%, $, millions); a correct method can still earn marks if the arithmetic slips.
For 15-mark evaluation questions, weigh both sides with stakeholders, short versus long run and assumptions, then reach a clear judgement.
Define the key term in the question, then build a step-by-step chain of reasoning; vague lists of points score poorly.
